Sportsmanship and manners in the squad

On the stand the key person is the referee. The referee looks after safety and order and judges each target.

The referee decides alone. Squad members do not say whether a target was hit unless the referee asks them. If other shooters openly criticise a decision (in Compak® Sporting, spectators too), the rules call it an attempt to influence the referee, and it is penalised. Losing self-control, such as throwing a gun or insulting anyone, is reported to the jury (the officials in charge of the competition). The jury can expel the shooter from the competition.

Disagree with a decision? Raise your hand at once, on the stand, and say “protest” or “appeal”. In Compak® Sporting do it before the next shooter calls for a target. If the referee is sure of what they saw, the decision stays as it is, and that is the end of it. The full procedure is in Results, protests and appeals.

Then carry on shooting calmly. Arguing further, by words or gestures, or challenging decisions for show, counts as an attempt to influence the referee, and penalties apply.

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™, check your score on the card when you leave each stand. Raise any disagreement with the referee at once: the referee alone decides, and there is no appeal afterwards.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 16 · Recording results and checking your score

Compak® Sporting

In Compak® Sporting, nobody may coach a shooter during the competition: the shooter gets a yellow card, and the adviser is sent out of the shooting area. Once shooting has started again after a decision, arguing about it counts as trying to influence the referee. So does open criticism of a decision by a shooter or a spectator. Either can get you excluded from the competition. At the end of each round you sign the score sheet (the card with your results). If you refuse to sign, no complaint from you can be accepted afterwards.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 15 · Signing the score sheet

Punctuality is the first courtesy in a squad, the group of at most six shooters you shoot with. Being late is also against the rules, and targets you miss while late can be scored as zeros: see The call, time limits and lateness. In Compak® Sporting you must report to the referee before the round. The shooting order changes during the round, so follow the rotation (the order in which the squad takes turns) and step up only when the stand is free.

Beyond the rules there are customs. Shooters usually greet the referee and the squad at the start. They say “good shot” or “well shot” after a good stand and “bad luck” after a miss. Comments on someone’s technique, unless they ask, are usually not welcome. A word of thanks to the trapper and referee at the end, a handshake, and calm when results go up are common at many shooting grounds.

Referees often work all day in sun or rain, and at club shoots many referees are volunteers. Thanking them after the round is a small habit that means a lot. In clay shooting, rivals are often friends too.

Key points

  • The referee decides alone, and the decision is final
  • Disagree? Raise your hand at once and say “protest” or “appeal”
  • Further arguing counts as an attempt to influence the referee
  • Be on time (in Compak® Sporting, report to the referee before the round): if you are late, missed targets can count as zeros
  • Customs: greet, “well shot”, thank the trapper and referee

Did you know?

In both disciplines a shooter may not go and pick up a target to check whether it was hit: only the referee decides. In Sporting™, calling for the next target counts as accepting the last decision.

Stand Talk

  • Referee Number twelve — last call!

    Meaning: The referee is calling a missing shooter; if he does not come, his targets will be zeros.

  • Referee You’re next — get ready.

    Meaning: Prepare now: glasses, ears, cartridges, but do not step up until the stand is free.

  • Shooter Well shot!

    Meaning: Sincere praise after a good target or stand.

  • Shooter Bad luck.

    Meaning: Friendly sympathy after a miss, not criticism.

  • Shooter Thanks, ref — thanks for pulling.

    Meaning: Thanking the referee and the trapper at the end of the round.

For the interpreter
  • Translate these courtesies warmly: they matter to the squad. Pass on the referee’s decisions at once and word for word, and do not add your own opinion of them.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. Who decides whether a target was hit?

    1. The squad, by a show of hands
    2. The referee, and the referee alone
    3. The shooter, by checking the pieces
    Answer

    The referee, and the referee alone

    Only the referee decides; the squad does not step in unless the referee asks.

  2. How do you properly disagree with a referee’s decision?

    1. At once on the stand: raise your hand and say “protest”
    2. After the round, with a post on social media
    3. By arguing until the referee changes his mind
    Answer

    At once on the stand: raise your hand and say “protest”

    A protest is made at once, on the stand; arguing afterwards counts as an attempt to influence.

  3. A squad-mate loudly tells the referee he is wrong about a hit. How do the rules see this?

    1. As useful information for the referee
    2. As a formal protest by the squad
    3. As an attempt to influence the referee
    4. As normal chat with no consequence
    Answer

    As an attempt to influence the referee

    Others openly criticising a ruling without the referee’s permission count as an attempt to influence; only the shooter concerned may protest.
